subject: mathematics
question_text: If A + B + C = π, show that cos(A/2) + cos(B/2) − cos(C/2) = 4 cos((π + A)/4) cos((π + B)/4) cos((π − C)/4).

mark_split.label: Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula
Apply the product formula and conclude

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.100, chapter 8 TRANSFORMATIONS, Long Answer question 3(ii). The book prints TRANSFORMATIONS as a separate un-numbered chapter-style banner immediately after chapter 8's VSAQ run and restarts its numbering at 1; we ship both under one unit, ordered by the syllabus, and never mirror the book's arrangement. NUMBERING RECORDED, NOT RENUMBERED: the page prints "3. If A + B + C = π then show that" followed immediately by ii); no i) identity is printed anywhere under question 3, and the run is recorded as the book sets it. The printed right-hand side checks out exactly as printed — the equivalent form 4 sin((π−A)/4) sin((π−B)/4) cos((π−C)/4) is the same number, since sin θ = cos(π/2 − θ) sends (π−A)/4 to (π+A)/4; this card proves the printed cosine form directly. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+3+2+1+1 split rewards the two substantial transformations — the sum-to-product pairing and the use of the angle condition — over the set-up and the finish, and it is the same split and the same step ids already carried by the sibling cards of this family (sin2a_sum, cos2a_sum, sin_half_squares, cos_half_squares), deliberately: they are ONE method over different identities, so a student who learns the arc once can attempt any of them. IDENTITY CHECKED NUMERICALLY before and after writing, and every intermediate line of the derivation with it: at A = 50°, B = 60°, C = 70° both sides equal 0.9531811465, and the identity holds again at (40°, 75°, 65°) and (110°, 25°, 45°). Paper position: Maths-1A Section C carries the long answers at 8 marks each under the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27), any 2 of 3; the Transformations slot is always a question of this kind. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the angle condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. The right-hand side is built from QUARTER angles, so the condition is not only stated but divided by 4 before it is used.
steps.memory_tip: Every argument on the right has a 4 under it, so divide the condition by 4: (A+B)/4 = (π−C)/4.
lines: A + B + C = π  ⇒  A + B = π − C

recall.must_convey: That the condition is divided by 4, giving (A+B)/4 = (π−C)/4, because the right-hand side is in quarter angles.
accept: divide the angle sum by four to get A plus B over four equals pi minus C over four
quarter the condition because the answer is in quarter angles
write the condition down and bring it to quarter angles
condition ni four tho divide chesi, A plus B by four equals pi minus C by four rasi
state the given condition in quarter angle form

steps.why: The condition can only be substituted into an expression of the same size, so it is brought down to quarter angles at the start.
common_mistakes: Halving the condition instead of quartering it.
Writing the condition but never rearranging it into a usable form.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Three of the eight marks. Pair the two PLUS terms; averaging two half angles is where the quarter angles first appear. Then cos(C/2) is rewritten as a product of two quarter-angle factors.
steps.memory_tip: Pairing two half angles halves them again — that is where the quarter angles come from.
lines: [∵ cos p + cos q = 2 cos((p+q)/2) cos((p−q)/2)]

recall.must_convey: That cos(A/2) and cos(B/2) are paired with the cos C + cos D formula, and cos(C/2) is written as 2 sin((π−C)/4) cos((π−C)/4).
accept: pair the two plus terms with the cosine sum formula, which gives quarter angles
apply sum to product on cos A over two and cos B over two
write cos C over two as two sin pi minus C over four times cos pi minus C over four
modati rendu plus terms ni pair cheyyali, quarter angles vasthayi
expand cos C over two into quarter angle factors

steps.why: The sum formula averages the two arguments, so pairing cos(A/2) with cos(B/2) produces (A+B)/4 and (A−B)/4 by itself. The third term is brought to the same quarter size so it can share a factor.
common_mistakes: Applying the cosine SUM formula to a pair where one term carries a minus sign.
Writing (A+B)/2 instead of (A+B)/4 as the averaged argument.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. The quartered condition replaces (A+B)/4 by (π−C)/4, and the expansion of cos(C/2) is substituted, so every term now carries cos((π−C)/4).
steps.memory_tip: After the substitution every term carries cos((π−C)/4). That is the factor that will come out.

recall.must_convey: That (A+B)/4 is replaced by (π−C)/4 and the expansion of cos(C/2) is put in, so both terms carry cos((π−C)/4).
accept: replace A plus B over four by pi minus C over four
substitute the condition so both terms carry cos pi minus C over four
put in the expansion of cos C over two as well
A plus B by four ni pi minus C by four ga marchali
use the quartered condition to convert the first term

steps.why: The condition converts an expression in A and B into one in C. Only then do the two terms share a common factor.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to substitute the expansion of cos(C/2) as well as the condition.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. The common factor 2 cos((π−C)/4) comes out, and the sine inside the bracket is turned into a cosine so that the bracket becomes a SUM of two cosines.
steps.memory_tip: cos(θ + π/2) = −sin θ turns the minus sine inside the bracket into a plus cosine.

recall.must_convey: That 2 cos((π−C)/4) is taken out and −sin((π−C)/4) is rewritten as cos((2π+A+B)/4), so the bracket is a sum of cosines.
accept: take two cos pi minus C over four common and turn the sine into a cosine
use cos of theta plus pi by two equals minus sine theta so the bracket adds
the bracket becomes cos A minus B over four plus cos two pi plus A plus B over four
two cos pi minus C by four common teesi, sine ni cosine ga marchali
rewrite the sine as a cosine so both bracket terms match

steps.why: Both bracket terms must be cosines before a formula applies, and the bracket must be a SUM, because only a sum of cosines gives the product of cosines the right-hand side needs.
common_mistakes: Writing cos(θ + π/2) = +sin θ and leaving the bracket as a difference.

steps.label: Apply the product formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The cosine SUM formula turns the bracket into a product of two quarter-angle cosines. Half the sum gives (π+A)/4 and half the difference gives −(π+B)/4; cosine is an even function, so the minus sign disappears.
steps.memory_tip: Half the sum is (π+A)/4 and half the difference is −(π+B)/4. Cosine is even, so the minus sign drops.
lines: [∵ cos p + cos q = 2 cos((p+q)/2) cos((p−q)/2)]

recall.must_convey: That the cosine sum formula turns the bracket into 2 cos((π+A)/4) cos((π+B)/4), giving 4 cos((π+A)/4) cos((π+B)/4) cos((π−C)/4).
accept: apply the cosine sum formula to get two cos pi plus A over four times cos pi plus B over four
half the sum is pi plus A over four and half the difference is pi plus B over four
the bracket becomes a product of two quarter angle cosines so the answer is four of them
cos sum formula tho two cos pi plus A by four cos pi plus B by four vasthundi
the final answer is four cos pi plus A by four cos pi plus B by four cos pi minus C by four

steps.why: A sum of two cosines is a product of two cosines. Averaging (A−B)/4 with (2π+A+B)/4 gives (π+A)/4, and their half difference gives (π+B)/4 once the even property of cosine is used.
common_mistakes: Using the cosine difference formula, which would give sines.
Keeping the minus sign on −(π+B)/4 instead of using that cosine is even.
